claims.text: A model explicitly incorporating random atomic disorder and defect states will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than perfect-crystal models.
Oxygen contamination induces defect states relevant to electrical conduction in HfNbTaTiZr.
Between 0 and 200 K, conduction is dominated by thermal activation of carriers from defect-induced localized levels.
Between 300 and 1200 K, conduction becomes intrinsic and is modified by oxygen-related lattice distortions that alter the effective band gap.
Spark plasma sintering of gas-atomized HfNbTaTiZr powders can produce bulk material containing approximately 0.12 wt.% oxygen.
A disordered-structure model with defect-level statistics can represent oxygen-induced defects and grain-boundary effects.
Oxygen induces lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen can produce oxygen vacancies, other defect states, and possibly secondary nanophases in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defects mediate carrier scattering and modify the band structure.
The activation energy for low-temperature defect-level conduction is lower than the intrinsic band gap.
At 300–1200 K, oxygen-induced mid-gap states enhance thermal excitation from the valence band to the conduction band.
Oxygen-induced mid-gap states modify the effective band gap and carrier concentration relative to a perfect crystal.
Arrhenius plots of conductivity will exhibit distinct activation energies in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
At 0–200 K, the advanced model will predict conductivities several orders of magnitude lower than conventional models.
At 300–1200 K, oxygen-induced modifications will moderate the rate at which conductivity increases with temperature.
The advanced model will closely reproduce conductivity measurements from the specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen across both temperature regimes.
Perfect, defect-free crystal models tend to overestimate mobility and conductivity, especially between 0 and 200 K.
Perfect-crystal models fail to capture oxygen-induced changes in high-temperature conduction pathways.
The proposed method is applicable from 0 to 1200 K at approximately ambient pressure to bulk, single-phase, powder-metallurgy HfNbTaTiZr containing up to about 1 wt.% oxygen.
The method may not apply under substantially elevated pressure or when extensive second-phase precipitation is present.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says oxygen-induced mid-gap states enhance high-temperature carrier excitation, whereas the predicted outcome says oxygen moderates the conductivity increase. These effects could coexist through a mobility–carrier-concentration tradeoff, but that tradeoff is not stated, leaving the direction of the oxygen effect internally ambiguous.

The low-temperature mechanism invokes defect levels with a lower activation energy than the intrinsic gap, which ordinarily facilitates carrier activation, while the outcome attributes conductivity that is several orders of magnitude lower specifically to those defect levels. A sufficiently large mobility or carrier-density reduction could reconcile the statements, but it is not quantified or explicitly linked.

The central hypothesis concerns improved predictive accuracy, but the falsification rule tests whether measurements differ from conventional-model values rather than whether the advanced model has lower held-out prediction error. Measurements could differ from the conventional model while also disagreeing with the advanced model, so the stated rule is not decisive for the claimed accuracy advantage.
